## Roadmap {.smaller}

Six parts. Parts I–IV are the standard story — the one in any textbook.
Parts V–VI are about the four cores on the desk in front of you.

**The stock story**

1. **Why a hierarchy exists** — the technology, and the economics
2. **Locality** — the empirical fact that makes it work
3. **AMAT** — the one equation
4. **The mechanisms** — direct-mapped, block size, associativity, replacement, write policy

**Our silicon**

5. **Four cores, four answers** — C906 ×2, Cortex-A53, Ryzen 7 9850X3D
6. Synthesis

::: {.notes}
Frame the deck: two halves, and the second half is why the first half is worth learning.
Everything in Parts I–IV will be tested; everything in Part V is what makes it stick,
because it is about the chip in their hand.

Do not let the deck become a tour of MIT's slides. Every mechanism gets taught from
scratch, then immediately grounded in our hardware.
:::

# Part 0 — Framing

## The Gap {.smaller}

A core at 1 GHz retires an instruction every **1 ns**. That is the clock we build the
pipeline around. Now look at what memory costs:

| Level | Latency | In 1 GHz core cycles |
|---|---|---|
| Register file | ~0 | **0** |
| L1 SRAM | 1–4 ns | **1–4** |
| L2 (A53 only) | ~10 ns | **~10** |
| DDR3, random access | 60–100 ns | **60–100** |
| SPI NAND, page read | 50–100 µs | **50,000–100,000** |

::: {.fragment}
A program that missed on *every* access would run a hundred times slower than the core
is capable of. No amount of pipelining, branch prediction, or superscalar width fixes
that — the core would simply sit idle.
:::

::: {.notes}
The 1 ns figure is the whole motivation. Say it out loud: "the CPU can start a new
instruction every nanosecond, and DRAM takes a hundred."

Note the last row: SPI NAND is five orders of magnitude off the core. That is why
"just put the program in flash and run it" does not work, and why everything gets
copied into DRAM at boot — which they saw in the boot deck.

Caveat to state honestly: the DDR3 number is an estimate from CAS latency plus tRCD
plus controller overhead, not a measurement. We will come back to it in Part III.
:::

## What a Level Must Buy {.smaller}

Every storage technology is characterised by four numbers. The MIT table, with ours
alongside:

| | Capacity | Latency | Cost per bit | On our board |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Registers** | 1000s of bits | 20 ps | \$\$\$\$ | 31 × 64 b + PC |
| **SRAM** | 10 KB – 10 MB | 1–10 ns | \$\$\$ | 96 KB of L1 |
| **DRAM** | ~10 GB | 80 ns | \$ | 512 MB DDR3 |
| **Flash** | ~100 GB | 100 µs | ¢ | 16–64 GB NAND |
| **Disk** | ~1 TB | 10 ms | ¢ | eMMC, up to 2 TB |

::: {.fragment}
Read the table down the columns: every step down is roughly **10× more capacity for
10× more latency and 10× less cost per bit**. That is not a coincidence of
engineering — it is the physics of how you store a bit.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is MIT's slide 2/14 table, relabelled with our hardware. The point to land: the
trade is remarkably consistent across five orders of magnitude. Which means it is a
law, not a product decision.

The "cost per bit" column is the one students skip. Make them read it: DRAM is ~1000×
cheaper per bit than SRAM. That is the reason a 512 MB SRAM does not exist, and no
amount of cleverness will make one.
:::

## The Promise {.smaller}

The hierarchy is not a memory. It is an **illusion generator**: a small, fast, expensive
memory that *behaves* like a large, fast, cheap one.

Three claims, and the rest of the lecture is support for them:

1. **A large fast memory cannot be built.** (Part I)
2. **Programs have locality, so a small fast memory suffices.** (Part II)
3. **We can quantify how well it works, and tune it.** (Parts III–IV)

::: {.fragment}
Claim 2 is the one that could have been false. It is an empirical fact about real
programs, not a theorem — and it is the fact the entire memory hierarchy rests on.
:::

::: {.notes}
Flag claim 2 hard. If programs accessed memory uniformly at random, caches would buy
exactly nothing, and every technique in this lecture would be pointless. Locality is
the load-bearing assumption.

It is also an assumption programmers can break, and do — which is why the later
material on conflict misses and working sets matters.
:::

## What We Will Not Do Today {.smaller}

- **Virtual memory.** Translation, page tables, page faults — that is a later deck.
  We will only touch the MMU where it forces a cache design decision.
- **Coherency.** Multiple cores, multiple caches, who wins. Named, not solved.
- **The lab.** How you measure any of this on the board is a separate conversation.

::: {.fragment}
What we *will* do: build the whole standard model from the transistor up, and then
check it against four real cores — two of which are on the same die and disagree with
each other.
:::

::: {.notes}
Scope-setting. Students will ask about virtual memory immediately because the C906 has
an MMU and a TLB; defer it explicitly.

The "two cores on the same die disagree" line is the hook for Part V. Do not explain
it yet.
:::

# Part I — Why a Hierarchy Exists

## Four Ways to Store a Bit {.smaller}

Everything below follows from *how many devices it takes to hold one bit*.

| | Devices per bit | Access time | Volatile | Writes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SRAM** | **6 transistors** | 1–10 ns | yes | unlimited |
| **DRAM** | **1 transistor + 1 capacitor** | ~80 ns | yes | unlimited |
| **Flash** | 1 floating gate | 10–100 µs | **no** | **~10³–10⁵, then worn out** |
| **Disk** | a magnetic domain | 10 ms | no | unlimited |

::: {.fragment}
Six devices versus two. That ratio — roughly **20× density** — is the entire reason
DRAM exists and SRAM does not simply scale up.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide is the physical foundation for everything after. The columns that matter:
devices per bit explains density and cost; volatility explains why flash needs no
refresh but has endurance limits; write endurance explains why you do not put a
swap file on raw NAND without a flash translation layer.

Note the flash endurance column — it is the one that bites in practice, and it is why
the root filesystem on their boards is not written to casually.
:::

## SRAM: the 6T Cell {.smaller}

Two CMOS inverters wired into a loop — the output of each drives the input of the other.
That loop has **two stable states**, and those two states are a bit.

Two more transistors connect the loop to a pair of **bitlines**, gated by a **wordline**:

```text
        wordline
           |
   BL ──[access]──+---------+──[access]── BL̄
                  |         |
                [inv]     [inv]
                  |         |
                  +---------+
                (cross-coupled: bistable)
```

::: {.fragment}
Six transistors, and the bit is held by feedback — no refresh, no capacitor, and
reading it does not destroy it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Draw this on the chalkboard rather than pointing at the ASCII. The key insight is
"bistable": two inverters in a ring have two fixed points, so the cell remembers.

Contrast with a latch: this is the same idea as the D-latch from the sequential logic
deck, minus the clock, with the access transistors playing the role of the gate.
:::

## SRAM: Reading and Writing {.smaller}

**Read** — precharge both bitlines high and let them float, raise the wordline, and let
the cell pull *one* bitline down. A sense amplifier resolves the small difference.

- The cell only *pulls down*; it never drives high. So the read is **non-destructive**.

**Write** — drive the bitlines hard to the desired values, raise the wordline, and
**overpower** the cell's feedback loop so it flips.

::: {.fragment}
The access transistors must be sized so that a bitline at 0 can overpower a cell holding
1 — but a bitline at 1 must *not* overpower a cell holding 0.

**Why the asymmetry?** *(Think about it before the next slide.)*
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT poses this as an open question on slide 6, and it is a genuinely good one. The
answer: reads and writes share the same access transistors, and a read is just "let the
cell fight the precharged bitline". If the access transistor were symmetric and strong
enough to write a 1 over a stored 0, then a read of a stored 0 would be flipped by the
precharged-high bitline — reads would destroy data.

So the sizing is a compromise: strong enough to write, weak enough not to corrupt on
read. Real designs use a write-assist (lowering the cell supply during write) to widen
the margin.

Do not give the answer immediately — let them guess. It is the best discussion moment
in Part I.
:::

## Why SRAM Cannot Be Large {.smaller}

Two limits, both physical:

1. **Six transistors per bit.** A 64 KB cache is half a million transistors before you
   count the tags, the decoders, or the sense amps.
2. **Wires dominate.** An *N*-entry multiported SRAM needs *N* wordlines and *2N*
   bitlines crossing the array. The wire area grows as **O(N²)**.

::: {.fragment}
This is why "just make the L1 bigger" is not free, and why register files are tiny
and multiported while caches are large and single-ported.
:::

::: {.notes}
The O(N²) argument is MIT slide 7 and it is worth doing on the board: double the number
of entries and the bitlines double in length *and* in count, so the wire area
quadruples.

This is also the honest answer to "why is my L1 only 32 KB when I have 512 MB of RAM" —
it is not cost, it is that the access time of a big array is set by the wire delay to
the far corner.
:::

## DRAM: the 1T Cell {.smaller}

One transistor and one capacitor. The charge on the capacitor *is* the bit.

```text
   wordline
      |
   BL ──[access]──┤├── ground
              (capacitor)
```

Consequences, all of them annoying:

- The capacitor **leaks** — every cell must be **refreshed** every few milliseconds.
- Reading **shares charge** between the capacitor and the bitline — so the read is
  **destructive**, and the value must be written back.
- The voltage swing is tiny, so every bitline needs a **sense amplifier**.

::: {.fragment}
~20× denser than SRAM, and 2–10× slower. That is the trade, and it is a good one for
main memory.
:::

::: {.notes}
The capacitor is why DRAM is cheap: one transistor instead of six. The capacitor is also
why DRAM is slow and complicated: leak, refresh, destructive read, sense amps.

The trench capacitor detail from MIT's slide 9 is worth one sentence — to get enough
capacitance in a small area you dig a deep trench or stack layers, which is a
three-dimensional structure in a nominally planar process.
:::

## Flash and Disk {.smaller}

**Flash** — a floating gate traps electrons. Trapped charge means the transistor never
inverts, so the cell reads as permanently off. No power needed to hold the bit.

- Very dense, non-volatile, **no refresh**
- Slow to write (10–100 µs), and writing *damages* the oxide: **~10³–10⁵ cycles**

**Disk** — a magnetic domain, read by a head on a moving arm.

- ~10 ms to move the head: **five orders of magnitude** worse than DRAM
- But ~100× cheaper per bit, and it does not wear out

::: {.fragment}
Flash and disk are why the hierarchy continues below DRAM — and why "swap" exists.
:::

::: {.notes}
The endurance number matters practically: it is why SD cards die, and why the Debian
image on their board runs from eMMC or an SD card rather than raw NAND.

Do not spend long here. The point is only that the hierarchy keeps going in both
directions: registers above, flash and disk below.
:::

## Size Is a Fundamental Limit {.smaller}

> "Size is a fundamental limit, even setting cost aside."

Why: a bigger array means **longer bitlines**, which means **more capacitance**, which
means a **smaller voltage swing**, which takes **longer to sense**.

Latency grows with capacity **by physics**, not by bad engineering. You cannot buy your
way out of it with a bigger budget or a better process node.

::: {.fragment}
So a large, fast memory is impossible. If we want the *behaviour* of one, we have to
fake it — and that is what the rest of this lecture is about.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is MIT slide 14 and it is the pivot of Part I. Everything before it was "why each
technology is the way it is"; this is "and therefore the hierarchy is not optional".

Say it plainly: there is no future process node at which a 512 MB SRAM with 1-cycle
access appears. The wire delay alone forbids it.
:::

## ...Unless You Stack It {.smaller}

The 2026 answer to "size is a fundamental limit" was not to scale the array. It was to
put a **second die on top of it**.

AMD's 3D V-Cache: a separate silicon die containing **64 MB of SRAM**, bonded directly
underneath the compute die and wired into the L3.

- Ryzen 7 9850X3D: 32 MB of on-die L3 **+ 64 MB stacked = 96 MB**
- Same physics, different trick — the hierarchy got deeper by **packaging**

::: {.fragment}
MIT's 2017 deck says size is a fundamental limit. The industry's response was to stop
fighting it and start stacking.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the bridge into Part V and it is the most modern thing in the deck. The
teaching point: the constraint from the previous slide is real, and engineers routed
around it rather than through it.

Also worth noting the numbers for scale, which we will use again: 96 MB of L3 on that
part, versus 512 MB of *main memory* on our board. Their cache is about a fifth the
size of our entire DRAM.

Do not claim 3D V-Cache is transparent to software — it is, largely, but the OS needs
to know which cores are near which cache. One sentence, move on.
:::

# Part II — Locality

## The Locality Principle {.smaller}

> Access to address *X* at time *t* implies access to *X + ΔX* at time *t + Δt*
> becomes **more probable** as *ΔX* and *Δt* approach zero.

Two special cases, and both matter:

- **Temporal locality** — ΔX = 0. You will touch *the same* address again soon.
- **Spatial locality** — Δt = 0. You will touch a *nearby* address soon.

::: {.fragment}
This is an **empirical claim about real programs**, not a theorem. Compilers and
programmers *create* it — and sometimes destroy it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the statement carefully: it is a probability statement with two limits. MIT's
slide 17 states it exactly this way and the precision is the point.

Examples to give: temporal — a loop counter, a hot variable, an instruction in a loop
body. Spatial — walking an array, fetching sequential instructions.

The "programmers can destroy it" line sets up conflict misses later: a pointer-chasing
linked list has temporal locality but no spatial locality; a column-major walk of a
row-major matrix has neither.
:::

## Reference Patterns and the Working Set {.smaller}

Plot address against time and real programs do not fill the space — they draw
**bands and streaks**.

- Code: a few tight bands (the hot loops)
- Stack: a narrow band that moves slowly
- Data: streaks along the array being walked

Now pick a time window **Δt** and ask: how many *distinct* addresses were touched? Call
that set **S**, the **working set**.

::: {.fragment}
|S| grows as Δt grows, then **saturates** at the program's true footprint.

That saturation is the whole opportunity: **a cache bigger than the saturated working
set sees mostly hits.**
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slide 18. The graph is the important artefact — address on the vertical axis, time
on the horizontal, and the accesses forming clumps rather than a uniform fog.

The saturation is the punchline. It says the working set is *bounded* even though the
program runs for an unbounded time. That is why a 64 KB cache can serve a program that
touches gigabytes.

Ask the class: what does the curve look like for a program that streams a 3 MB video
frame once? Answer: |S| never saturates — no reuse, so no locality, and the cache cannot
help. That is exactly why the engines use DMA and carveouts instead (see the power deck).
:::

## Everything Is a Cache for Something Else {.smaller}

| Level | Size (ours) | Latency | Managed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registers | 1 KB | 0 cycles | **compiler** |
| L1 I / D | 32 KB / 64 KB | 1–4 cycles | hardware |
| L2 | 128 KB *(A53 only)* | ~10 cycles | hardware |
| L3 | **none** | — | — |
| Main memory | 512 MB DDR3 | 60–100 cycles | OS + hardware |
| Flash (NAND / eMMC) | 16 GB – 2 TB | 50–100 µs | OS |
| Network / cloud | ∞ | ms–s | distributed system |

::: {.fragment}
Each level is a cache for the level below it. The register file is a cache for the L1;
the L1 is a cache for DRAM; DRAM is a cache for flash.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is MIT slide 20 with our column filled in, and the filled-in column is the slide's
value: no L3, and an L2 that exists on only one of the four cores.

The "managed by" column is the one students have not thought about. Registers are
allocated by the compiler — that is a cache replacement policy implemented in software,
and it is why register allocation is a hard compiler problem. Flash-to-DRAM is managed
by the OS page cache. Same problem, three different owners.
:::

## Expose or Hide? {.smaller}

Two ways to give a programmer a hierarchy:

**Expose it.** "Here are two memories. Put the hot data in the fast one yourself."
Scratchpad memory, DSPs, some GPUs, and — partly — our **ION carveouts**.

**Hide it.** One flat address space. Hardware (and the OS) decide where data lives.
That is a **cache**.

::: {.fragment}
Every real system does **both**. Ours does both: the caches hide, and the carveouts
expose.
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slides 15–16 frame this as the interface question, and it is a good one because it
is a *design* choice with no universally right answer.

Exposed memory is predictable — a scratchpad has no conflict misses, so a real-time
audio pipeline can bound its worst case. Hidden memory is easier to program and usually
faster on average.

Tie to our board: ION carves DRAM out and hands it to the video pipeline as physically
contiguous buffers. That is an exposed hierarchy: the driver decides what goes there.
The caches are the hidden half. Students saw this in the power deck; this is the same
idea from the other direction.
:::

# Part III — AMAT: The One Equation

## Hit, Miss, and Two Ratios {.smaller}

A cache is asked for an address. There are exactly two outcomes:

| Outcome | What happens | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Hit** | the block is present; return it | hit time (a few cycles) |
| **Miss** | not present; fetch the block, evict something, return it | hit time + miss penalty |

- **Hit ratio (HR)** = hits / total accesses
- **Miss ratio (MR)** = 1 − HR

::: {.fragment}
The processor now has **variable** memory access time, and something has to cope with
that — either stall the pipeline, or keep going out of order.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is MIT slide 21. The point about variable latency is the one students underrate:
a cache turns a fixed-cost memory into a variable-cost memory, and the whole
microarchitecture has to absorb the variance. That is why an in-order core with a
cache miss is so much slower than an out-of-order one.

Our C906 is in-order. A miss there is a hard stall — no other work to do. Worth
saying, and worth connecting to the pipelining material.
:::

## AMAT {.smaller}

The **average memory access time**:

$$\text{AMAT} = \text{HitTime} + \text{MissRatio} \times \text{MissPenalty}$$

Read it as: *every* access pays the hit time, and a fraction of them pay the penalty
on top.

::: {.fragment}
Two reasons this is the right metric:

- It is **per access**, so it multiplies cleanly by the instruction count.
- It **composes** — the miss penalty of one level is the AMAT of the next.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not let them memorise this without understanding the shape. The key structure: hit
time is paid unconditionally; the penalty is paid conditionally.

A useful sanity check to do on the board: if HR = 1, AMAT = HitTime. If HR = 0,
AMAT = HitTime + MissPenalty, which should equal the raw memory latency — and it does,
if HitTime is small relative to the penalty.

AMAT is what MIT slide 22 introduces and returns to on slides 28, 34, and 40. It is the
spine of the lecture; point that out so they notice the recurrence.
:::

## AMAT Composes {.smaller}

The miss penalty of level 1 is the AMAT of level 2:

$$\text{AMAT} = \text{HT}_1 + \text{MR}_1 \times
  \bigl(\text{HT}_2 + \text{MR}_2 \times \text{Penalty}_{\text{mem}}\bigr)$$

Now apply it to our two big cores, with the same L1 hit ratio of **0.95**:

| Core | Hierarchy | AMAT |
|---|---|---|
| **C906** | L1 → DDR3 | `2 + 0.05 × 80` = **6.0** cycles |
| **A53** | L1 → L2 → DDR3 | `2 + 0.05 × (10 + 0.20 × 80)` = **3.3** cycles |

::: {.fragment}
Same L1. Same hit ratio. The L2 nearly **halves** the AMAT — because it catches most of
the 5% that miss L1.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the most important quantitative slide in the deck, because it explains why the
A53 feels so much faster than the C906 at the same clock and with the same L1 sizes.

Walk the arithmetic slowly. Inside the bracket: a miss in L1 costs the L2 hit time (10)
plus, 20% of the time, the full memory penalty (80). That is 10 + 16 = 26. Multiply by
the 5% L1 miss rate: 1.3 cycles on top of 2.

For the C906 there is no bracket — the 5% miss pays the whole 80 cycles.

The numbers 10 and 80 are illustrative, not measured. The *structure* is the lesson:
a second level exists to shorten the bracket.
:::

## What Hit Ratio Do You Need? {.smaller}

Suppose a hit costs 2 cycles and a miss costs 100.

| Target | Equation | Required HR |
|---|---|---|
| **Beat no cache at all** (AMAT < 100) | `100 = 2 + (1−HR)·100` | **2%** |
| AMAT = 10 cycles | `10 = 2 + (1−HR)·100` | **92%** |
| AMAT = 5 cycles | `5 = 2 + (1−HR)·100` | **97%** |

::: {.fragment}
> Even a **terrible** cache beats no cache. But a **good** one has to be very good
> indeed — the last few percent of hit ratio is where all the engineering lives.
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slide 23 uses 4 cycles for a hit and 100 for a miss, giving 4% and 99%. Our hit time
is lower, which lowers the bar: 2% instead of 4%. Show that the break-even point is
just HitTime / MissPenalty — so a faster hit time makes the cache more forgiving.

The pedagogical shape is the non-linearity: going from 92% to 97% only buys 5 cycles,
but going from 0% to 2% buys 98. Diminishing returns, which sets up the associativity
curve in Part IV.
:::

## The Honest Caveat {.smaller}

That "80 cycles" is an **estimate**, not a measurement. It is DDR3 CAS latency plus
tRCD plus controller scheduling, and the controller is allowed to reorder.

- **Bandwidth floor:** one 64-byte line at peak 1866 Mbps × 16 bit = 3.73 GB/s is
  `64 B ÷ 3.73 GB/s` ≈ **17 ns ≈ 17 cycles** at 1 GHz.
- **Latency** is several times that, because a single random read cannot use peak
  bandwidth.

::: {.fragment}
We do not need the exact number to reason about caches. We need the **shape**: hit time
is single digits, miss penalty is double digits.
:::

::: {.notes}
Be explicit that this is derived, not measured. The bandwidth figure is solid arithmetic
(1866 Mbps × 16 bits); the latency figure is an engineering estimate.

The distinction between latency and bandwidth is the thing to teach here, because
students conflate them constantly. Peak bandwidth is what you get with a long stream of
sequential requests; latency is what you pay for one lonely cache line. A cache miss is
the second case, so the bandwidth number is a lower bound on the cost, not an estimate
of it.

If anyone asks how you would actually measure it: that is the lab, and we are not doing
the lab today.
:::

# Part IV — How a Cache Works

## The Basic Algorithm {.smaller}

```text
on each access to address A:
    if the cache holds the block containing A:
        HIT   → return the data, a few cycles
    else:
        MISS  → choose a line to evict
              → fetch the block containing A from memory
              → place it in the cache
              → return the data
```

::: {.fragment}
The pseudocode hides the two questions that define a cache:

1. **How do we search?** → direct-mapped, set-associative, fully-associative
2. **Which line do we evict?** → the replacement policy
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slide 24 ends with exactly this question: "How do we search the cache?" That is the
pivot into the next four slides.

Everything in Part IV is an answer to question 1 or question 2. Say that explicitly, so
the section has a spine and is not a list of vocabulary.

There is a third question — when do we write to memory — which is the write policy,
later.
:::

## Direct-Mapped: the Simplest Search {.smaller}

**One place for each block.** Block number modulo the number of lines.

Each line stores a **valid bit**, a **tag**, and the **data**:

| index | valid | tag | data |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | `0x20000` | 64 bytes |
| 1 | 0 | — | — |
| 2 | 1 | `0x1F4A3` | 64 bytes |
| … | | | |
| 255 | 1 | `0x20001` | 64 bytes |

Search: **index the array, compare one tag.** That is a single comparator, not a search.

::: {.notes}
The genius of direct-mapped is that "search" degenerates to "compute an address and
check one tag". No comparators, no mux, no CAM. That is why it is fast and cheap.

Note the valid bit: on reset every tag is garbage, so the valid bit is what says
"trust me". Emphasise it — students forget it and then cannot explain a cold-start miss.
:::

## A Worked Lookup on Our D-Cache {.smaller}

Our L1 D-cache: **64 KB, 4-way, 64 B lines** ⇒ **256 sets**.
A 32-bit address splits as **tag 18 | index 8 | offset 6**.

| Address | offset | index | tag | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x8000_1040` | `0x00` | `0x41` (65) | `0x20000` | load it into set 65 |
| `0x8000_1040` again | `0x00` | `0x41` | `0x20000` | **HIT** |
| `0x8000_5040` | `0x00` | `0x41` | `0x20001` | different tag — **MISS** |

::: {.fragment}
Both addresses land in **set 65**. In a direct-mapped cache they would evict each other
forever. In ours, both can live there — we have four ways.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do this arithmetic live on the board; it is the single most useful mechanical skill in
the lecture. Write the address in binary, slice 6 bits off the bottom, then 8, and
everything left is the tag.

Check the second row explicitly: `0x8000_5040 − 0x8000_1040 = 0x4000 = 16384 = 256 × 64`.
So the two addresses are exactly 256 lines apart, which is why the index is identical.

The punchline is the fragment: this is a *conflict*, and associativity is the cure.
:::

## Part of the Address Is Encoded in the Location {.smaller}

The index bits are **not stored** anywhere. They are implied by *which line you looked
in* — the hardware computed them from the address.

So the tag array only needs the top bits:

| Cache | Sets × ways | Metadata per line | Tag array total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct-mapped 64 KB | 1024 × 1 | 18 tag + 1 valid + 1 dirty | **640 B** |
| Our 4-way 64 KB | 256 × 4 | 18 tag + 1 valid + 1 dirty | **2.5 KB** |

::: {.fragment}
> The address is partly stored **in the location**. That is what makes a cheap,
> one-comparator search possible — and it is also the source of conflict misses.
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slide 26 puts this in a red banner and it deserves the emphasis: "Part of the address
(index bits) is encoded in the location!"

The arithmetic: 256 sets × 4 ways × 20 bits = 20,480 bits = 2.5 KB, on top of 64 KB of
data. About 4% overhead. A direct-mapped cache of the same size needs only 640 B — a
quarter of the metadata, for a quarter of the flexibility.

This is also the intuition for why the tag can be small: 18 bits instead of a 32-bit
address.
:::

## Block Size: the Third Field {.smaller}

The address now has three fields, not two:

```text
 31                    14 13        6 5      0
+------------------------+-----------+--------+
|         tag (18)       | index (8) | off (6)|
+------------------------+-----------+--------+
```

The **block offset** selects a byte *inside* the line. It costs nothing to store —
it is pure address arithmetic — and it buys you spatial locality for free.

::: {.fragment}
So why not make blocks enormous? Because a bigger block means:

- **fewer blocks** for the same capacity → **more conflicts**
- a longer fill: you must fetch the *whole* line before you can use *any* of it
- wasted bandwidth if you never touch the rest of the line
:::

::: {.notes}
The three-field split is the single diagram to leave on the board for the rest of the
lecture. Everything else is a variation on it.

The "costs nothing to store" point is subtle and worth making: the offset bits are not
in the tag array, so a 64-byte block is 64× the data for the same tag storage. That is
why blocks exist at all.

The three costs in the fragment are the setup for the next slide's U-curve.
:::

## Block Size Tradeoffs {.smaller}

AMAT as a function of block size is **U-shaped**, because two effects fight:

| Block size | Miss rate | Miss penalty | AMAT |
|---|---|---|---|
| too small | high — no spatial reuse | small | **worse** |
| **~64 B** | minimum | moderate | **best** |
| too large | low | **large** — long fill, few blocks | **worse** |

::: {.fragment}
MIT's deck puts the optimum at about **64 bytes** (slide 28). Our C906's line size is
**exactly 64 bytes**, on both caches.

That is not a coincidence. It is the same optimum, found independently.
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slide 28 shows three curves — miss rate falling, miss penalty rising, and AMAT
U-shaped between them — with the minimum around 64 bytes. Draw the two components and
let the sum appear.

The reason the optimum is so stable across machines is that it is set by DRAM burst
length and by the granularity of spatial locality in real code, not by the cache.

Land the point: our hardware agrees with the textbook, which should increase their
confidence in the textbook. Later we will find places where it does not.
:::

## Conflict Misses {.smaller}

Misses come in three kinds:

- **Compulsory** (cold) — first touch. Unavoidable.
- **Capacity** — the working set is bigger than the cache. Unavoidable at that size.
- **Conflict** — the working set *fits*, but maps to too few sets. **Avoidable.**

A concrete case on our D-cache. A row of this matrix is exactly 16 KB:

```c
int A[1024][4096];        /* 4096 ints = 16 KB per row */
for (int i = 0; i < 1024; i++)
    sum += A[i][0];       /* walk one column */
```

::: {.fragment}
Every `A[i][0]` is 16 KB after the last — **256 lines apart** — so they all land in the
**same set**. Four fit in four ways. The fifth thrashes, forever.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is MIT slide 29's lesson (their version: two data arrays 1024 words apart all hit;
2048 words apart all miss) translated into our geometry, where the magic stride is
16 KB = 256 sets × 64 B.

The fix, for the record, is to pad the row length or transpose the loop. Say it, but do
not dwell — the point is that the programmer can create or destroy locality, which
recalls the Part II warning.

Ask: how many ways would you need to survive this? Answer: 1025 — i.e. fully
associative, i.e. the wrong fix. The right fix is to change the access pattern.
:::

## Fully Associative {.smaller}

**No index at all.** A block may live in *any* line.

To search, compare the tag against **every line in parallel** — that is a CAM, and it
costs one comparator and one tag read per line.

| | Direct-mapped | Fully associative |
|---|---|---|
| Search cost | 1 comparator | **N comparators** |
| Conflict misses | many | **none** |
| Data select | none | N:1 mux |

::: {.fragment}
Used where *N* is small and misses are expensive: our **μTLBs** are 10-entry fully
associative, and the **branch target buffer** is 16-entry fully associative.
:::

::: {.notes}
The CAM cost is the whole story: you cannot build a 256-entry fully associative cache
without 256 parallel comparators on the critical path, which is why real L1 caches are
never fully associative.

But our C906 does use it where it fits — the I-μTLB and D-μTLB are 10 entries each,
fully associative, and the BTB is 16 entries. Those are small enough that N comparators
is affordable, and misses there are expensive enough to be worth it.

Nice moment: the same design decision, made three times at three different scales on
the same core.
:::

## N-Way Set Associative {.smaller}

The compromise. Draw the cache as a **grid**:

```text
          way 0      way 1      way 2      way 3
set 0   [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ]
set 1   [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ]
set 2   [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ]
  ...      ...        ...         ...         ...
set 255 [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ] [ v|tag|d ]
```

A block maps to **one row** (chosen by the index) and may occupy **any column**.

::: {.fragment}
Direct-mapped is 1-way. Fully associative is 1 set.

It is exactly **N direct-mapped caches in parallel**, sharing an index.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is MIT slides 31–32. The grid is the right mental picture and it is worth drawing
properly: rows are sets, columns are ways, and a cache lookup touches an entire row.

The two degenerate cases are the point: the space of designs is one parameter, N, with
direct-mapped at one end and fully associative at the other. Students who see it that
way stop memorising three separate structures.
:::

## N-Way Structure {.smaller}

```text
address ──► [index] ──► select set (row)
                            │
              ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
              ▼             ▼             ▼
          [tag 0 ==]    [tag 1 ==]    [tag 2 ==]     ← N comparators, in parallel
              │             │             │
              └──── OR ─────┴──── OR ─────┘──► HIT
                            │
                       [N:1 mux] ──► data to CPU
```

::: {.fragment}
Cost: **N comparators and an N:1 mux on the critical path**. Hit time grows with N.

That is the tension: more ways means fewer conflict misses, but every access pays for
the extra comparators.
:::

::: {.notes}
The structure diagram explains the whole tradeoff in one picture: the comparators are
in parallel, so the delay is not N× a comparator, but it is an N-input OR tree plus an
N:1 mux, and both get slower as N grows.

Say clearly: this is why associativity is not free, and why the AMAT curve in the next
slide has a minimum rather than falling forever.
:::

## Associativity Tradeoffs {.smaller}

AMAT versus associativity is also **U-shaped**: conflict misses fall, hit time rises.

> "Little additional benefit beyond **4 to 8 ways**." — H&P, cited on MIT slide 34

Our four cores, all on the same curve:

| Core | L1 I | L1 D |
|---|---|---|
| C906 @ 700 MHz | 16 KB, **2-way** | 16 KB, **4-way** |
| C906 @ 1 GHz | 32 KB, **2-way** | 64 KB, **4-way** |
| Cortex-A53 | 32 KB, n/d | 32 KB, n/d |
| Ryzen 7 9850X3D | 32 KB, **8-way** | 48 KB, **12-way** |

::: {.fragment}
Zen 5 raised its L1 D-cache from 8-way to **12-way** specifically *to accommodate* the
larger 48 KB size. That is the tradeoff curve, visible in a shipping product.
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slide 34 is H&P Figure 5.9, and the quotation is the takeaway: beyond 4 to 8 ways
you are paying hit time for a shrinking benefit.

The Zen 5 detail is a lovely confirmation: AMD did not go to 12 ways for fun, they went
because they wanted 48 KB and 8-way would have made the conflict rate worse. That is
exactly the reasoning the lecture just taught, in a product launched in 2026.

Note the A53 row has no associativity — the SG2002 TRM documents only sizes. Flag it
as a gap rather than filling it in from memory. That is deliberate: a blank cell is a
fact about our sources, and a plausible-looking guess is a lie the students cannot
detect.
:::

## Replacement Policy {.smaller}

Only matters when ways > 1 — you must choose a victim.

| Policy | Rule | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Belady's MIN** | evict the block used *furthest in the future* | optimal; needs the future — **unimplementable** |
| **LRU** | evict the least recently used | good; needs ~log₂(N!) bits per set |
| **FIFO** | evict the longest-resident | cheap; log₂(N) bits — but **not a stack algorithm** |
| **Random** | evict at random | no state; no adversarial pattern |

::: {.fragment}
Belady's MIN is still useful: it is the **lower bound** you measure other policies
against.
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slide 36. The classification worth remembering: Belady is a bound, LRU is the
quality reference, FIFO and random are the cheap approximations.

Exact LRU for a 4-way set needs enough state to encode one of 4! = 24 orderings, i.e. 5
bits; FIFO needs 2. That is the cost side. Real hardware mostly uses pseudo-LRU
approximations because true LRU's bookkeeping is on the critical path.

Foreshadow: our C906 uses FIFO on *both* caches, and that has a consequence we will
look at in Part V.
:::

## Why FIFO Is Different {.smaller}

FIFO is **not a stack algorithm** — it does not obey the inclusion property. The
consequence is **Belady's anomaly**: giving it *more* capacity can make it *worse*.

Classic reference string, three frames versus four:

| Frames | Faults |
|---|---|
| 3 | **9** |
| 4 | **10** |

::: {.fragment}
More cache, more misses. LRU cannot do this — it is a stack algorithm, so a bigger
cache always contains the smaller one's contents.

In practice FIFO is usually fine. But "usually fine" is a different claim from
"cannot be worse", and our D-cache makes the weaker one.
:::

::: {.notes}
The reference string is `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5`. Walk it on the board if there is time
— it takes two minutes and students remember it for years, because it violates the
intuition that more memory is always at least as good.

Be fair to our hardware: Belady's anomaly is a capacity effect, and in a fixed 4-way
cache it is a curiosity rather than a practical problem. The honest statement is that
FIFO gives up a guarantee LRU has, and gains cheap bookkeeping in exchange.

This is the slide where "our silicon differs from the textbook" first bites, so it is
the natural bridge into Part V.
:::

## Write Policy {.smaller}

Reads are easy. Writes force a choice — and a second one on a write *miss*:

| Policy | On a write | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Write-through** | write cache *and* memory | simple, no dirty bit — but every store costs bandwidth |
| **Write-behind** | write a buffer, drain later | core does not stall; still full bandwidth |
| **Write-back** | write only the cache; memory on eviction | fastest, lowest bandwidth — needs a dirty bit |

And on a write miss: **write-allocate** (fetch the block first) or **write-no-allocate**
(write straight through)?

::: {.fragment}
Our C906 D-cache: **write-back**, with write-allocate / write-no-allocate
**configurable** — and an adaptive mode we will meet in Part V.
:::

::: {.notes}
MIT slide 37 presents the three policies with write-back marked "commonly implemented",
which is still true.

The second question — allocate or not on a write miss — is the one that matters more in
practice and gets less attention. If you are going to overwrite the entire line, fetching
it first is pure waste: you pay a memory read for data you are about to destroy. That is
why streaming stores exist, and why our chip has an adaptive mechanism.

Draw the connection: `memset` of a large buffer is the pathological case for
write-allocate.
:::

## Dirty Bits {.smaller}

One extra bit per line. It answers: *does memory match this line?*

- **WRITE** to a line → set `dirty = 1`
- **Evict** a line → write it back **only if** `dirty == 1`
- **Fill** a line from memory → `dirty = 0`

::: {.fragment}
The consequence is uncomfortable: **main memory can be stale.** DRAM is not the truth;
the cache is. Everything that bypasses the cache — DMA, another core, a debugger — now
has a coherency problem.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is MIT slides 38–39, and it is where the lecture connects to the power deck's DMA
material.

The uncomfortable consequence is the important one. Once you have a write-back cache,
"the value in memory" is a lie, and every agent that reads memory without going through
the cache has to be told. That is what `dma_sync_*` does in Linux, and it is why the
little C906 being non-coherent with the big core matters.

Also: this is why cache maintenance *instructions* exist at all — `DCACHE.CPA`,
`DCACHE.CIPA`, `ICACHE.IVA` and friends. They are the manual override for "make memory
true again". We are not doing the lab, but that is what they are for.
:::

# Part V — Four Cores, Four Answers

## Four Cores, Four Answers {.smaller}

Everything so far was the model. Here is what four real cores did with it.

| | **C906 @ 1 GHz** | **C906 @ 700 MHz** | **Cortex-A53** | **Ryzen 7 9850X3D** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L1 I** | 32 KB, 2-way | 16 KB, 2-way | 32 KB, n/d | 32 KB, 8-way |
| **L1 D** | 64 KB, 4-way | 16 KB, 4-way | 32 KB, n/d | 48 KB, 12-way |
| **L2** | — | — | **128 KB** | 1 MB, 16-way |
| **L3** | — | — | — | **96 MB** |
| **Line** | 64 B | 64 B | 64 B | 64 B |
| **Replacement** | FIFO | FIFO | n/d | n/d |
| **Prefetch** | yes, both | yes, both | n/d | yes |

::: {.fragment}
Associativity runs **2 → 4 → 8 → 12**. L3 runs **none → none → none → 96 MB**.

And the line size is **64 bytes on all four**. That is the one column where the entire
industry agrees.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff slide for the whole lecture. Every column is a design decision the
students can now name and justify.

The 64-byte line across all four is the strongest evidence for the block-size slide: it
is set by DRAM burst granularity and by the spatial locality of real code, and it has
been stable for two decades.

Three honesty notes. `n/d` means **not documented in the sources we had** — the SG2002
TRM gives the A53's sizes but not its associativity, and neither ARM's nor AMD's
replacement policy is documented in a form we could cite. A dash (`—`) means the level
does not exist. Keep those two symbols distinct; conflating them is how spec tables lie.
:::

## Two C906s, Not One {.smaller}

The SG2000 has **two** C906 cores, and they are not the same core:

| | Big C906 | Little C906 |
|---|---|---|
| Clock | 1.0 GHz | **700 MHz** |
| L1 I | 32 KB | **16 KB** |
| L1 D | 64 KB | **16 KB** |
| Runs | Linux | FreeRTOS / bare metal |
| MMU | yes | M-mode, physical |

::: {.fragment}
Half the clock — but **half the I-cache and a quarter of the D-cache**. A memory-bound
workload on the little core loses far more than 30%: it loses on capacity *and* on
latency at the same time.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a distinction students routinely miss — they see "2 × C906" in the SG2000
summary and assume two identical cores. The 700 MHz part has a much smaller cache, and
that is a bigger deal than the clock.

Note the trap: 700/1000 = 0.7, so a compute-bound workload loses 30%. But a
memory-bound workload loses more, because the smaller cache raises the miss ratio while
the slower clock raises the cycle time. Both penalties compound.

Also: the little core runs M-mode with physical addressing, so it has no MMU and no
TLB pressure — which means its cache behaviour is, if anything, simpler to reason about
than the big core's.
:::

## C906 L1 I-Cache: 2-Way {.smaller}

Straight from the manual (§7.1):

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Size | **8 / 16 / 32 / 64 KB**, hardware-configurable |
| Associativity | **2-way** set associative |
| Line | **64 B** |
| Indexing | **VIPT** — virtual index, physical tag |
| Read width | **32 bits** |
| Refill width | **128 bits** |
| Replacement | **FIFO** |
| Maintenance | whole-cache and single-line invalidate |
| Prefetch | yes — `MHINT.IPLD`, **same page only** |

::: {.fragment}
2-way is the **bottom of the useful range** — the minimum that removes the worst
conflict misses without paying for comparators on the fetch path.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the table. Two entries deserve comment.

The 32-bit read width with a 128-bit refill means the I-cache is filled four words at a
time but read one word at a time — a deliberate asymmetry, because refills are
bandwidth-bound and fetches are latency-bound.

The prefetch restriction to the same page is a safety feature: prefetching across a page
boundary could touch an address with no valid mapping. That is a *correctness*
constraint, not a performance one, and it is a nice example of a cache interacting with
virtual memory.

2-way is unusual for an I-cache. Note it and move on — the discussion comes in two
slides.
:::

## C906 L1 D-Cache: 4-Way {.smaller}

§7.2 — and note how much more there is to say than for the I-cache:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Size | **8 / 16 / 32 / 64 KB**, hardware-configurable |
| Associativity | **4-way** set associative |
| Line | **64 B** |
| Indexing | **VIPT** |
| Read / write width | 64 bits / **128 bits** |
| Write policy | **write-back**, write-allocate or write-no-allocate (configurable) |
| Replacement | **FIFO** |
| Prefetch | **sequential and strided** (stride ≤ 16 lines, forward *and* backward) |
| Extra | **adaptive write-allocate**; LR/SC local monitor |

::: {.fragment}
The D-cache is where the interesting engineering is. Every row past "line size" is an
optimization the I-cache does not need.
:::

::: {.notes}
The contrast with the previous slide is the point: the data side has five extra
mechanisms, because data access patterns are varied and instruction access patterns are
not.

The 128-bit write width matters for a different reason than the read width: it lets the
core commit two registers per cycle into the cache, which is what an in-order core needs
to keep a store pipeline busy.

Bidirectional strided prefetch is genuinely unusual — most prefetchers only go forward.
Backward prefetch helps with loops that walk down an array.

Mention LR/SC briefly: it is implemented as a monitor *inside the L1 D-cache*, and it
fails if the D-cache is disabled. That is a lovely example of an unrelated feature
(atomic operations) silently depending on a cache being switched on.
:::

## The Same Vendor Disagreed With Itself {.smaller}

Same die. Same vendor. Same 64-byte line. Same FIFO policy.

**I-cache: 2-way. D-cache: 4-way.**

The manual does not say why. Two hypotheses worth arguing about:

- The I-cache sits on the **fetch critical path** — every comparator added there delays
  every instruction fetch, so it is kept minimal.
- Instruction streams have **regular, sequential** access patterns with few conflicts,
  so the second pair of ways buys less than it costs.

::: {.fragment}
Which is it? Or is it neither? This is a design tradeoff you can now *argue about*,
which is the difference between knowing the vocabulary and knowing the subject.
:::

::: {.notes}
Deliberately present this as an open question rather than asserting a reason — the
manual genuinely does not explain it, and inventing a rationale would be teaching them
to make things up.

Let them argue. Both hypotheses are plausible and they are not mutually exclusive. The
stronger version of the second: an I-cache miss costs a full fetch stall, so hit time
dominates, so you minimise comparators.

This slide is the intellectual centre of Part V: the same engineers, given the same
toolkit, made different choices for the two halves of a Harvard cache.
:::

## The A53 Has an L2. We Don't. {.smaller}

| | C906 @ 1 GHz | Cortex-A53 @ 1 GHz |
|---|---|---|
| L1 I / D | 32 KB / 64 KB | 32 KB / 32 KB |
| L2 | **none** | **128 KB** |
| On an L1 miss | straight to DDR3 | L2 first |

Back to the AMAT composition, same 0.95 L1 hit ratio:

| | AMAT |
|---|---|
| C906: `2 + 0.05 × 80` | **6.0 cycles** |
| A53: `2 + 0.05 × (10 + 0.20 × 80)` | **3.3 cycles** |

::: {.fragment}
The C906 has **twice the L1 D-cache** and still loses, because there is nothing behind
it to absorb a miss.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the single most practically useful comparison in the deck, and it is not the one
students expect. The C906 has *more* L1 data cache than the A53 and is still the slower
core for memory-bound work.

The lesson: L1 capacity and L2 presence are not interchangeable, and the second level is
worth more than extra first-level ways or kilobytes, because it attacks the *penalty*
term rather than the miss rate.

Caveat clearly: 10 and 80 are illustrative. The structure is the claim, not the digits.
:::

## Our Bit Arithmetic {.smaller}

Apply the three-field split to all four of our caches. Line size is 64 B everywhere, so
the offset is always 6 bits:

| Core | Cache | Size | Ways | Sets | index | offset | tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C906 1 GHz | I | 32 KB | 2 | 256 | 8 | 6 | 18 |
| C906 1 GHz | D | 64 KB | 4 | 256 | 8 | 6 | 18 |
| C906 700 MHz | I | 16 KB | 2 | 128 | 7 | 6 | 19 |
| C906 700 MHz | D | 16 KB | 4 | 64 | 6 | 6 | 20 |

::: {.fragment}
Both 1 GHz caches land on **256 sets and 8 index bits** — different sizes, same geometry.
The 64 KB D-cache gets its extra capacity from the *fourth way*, not from more sets.
:::

::: {.notes}
The arithmetic: sets = size ÷ (ways × line). 32768 ÷ (2×64) = 256. 65536 ÷ (4×64) = 256.
16384 ÷ (2×64) = 128. 16384 ÷ (4×64) = 64.

The coincidence on the third row is genuinely useful pedagogically: the 1 GHz I and D
caches have the same index width, so the same address maps to the same set number in
both — which is irrelevant because they are separate caches, but it makes the point that
capacity can be bought with ways as well as with sets.

Two honesty notes. First, the C906 is RV64, so with a full 64-bit address the tag is
50 bits, not 18 — we use 32-bit addresses here to match the rest of the deck. Second,
these are *derived* numbers, not quoted from the manual; the manual gives sizes, ways,
and line size, and the rest is arithmetic.
:::

## VIPT: Why the Index Can Be Virtual {.smaller}

**VIPT** = virtual index, physical tag. Why bother?

```text
virtual address ──┬──► [ index ] ──────────────► select set  ──┐
                  │                                            ├──► compare
                  └──► [ TLB ] ──► physical ──► [ tag ] ───────┘
                                    (in parallel)
```

The index needs no translation, so the **TLB lookup and the set selection run at the
same time**. With a physical index you would have to translate first, then index — two
serial latencies on every access.

::: {.fragment}
**The constraint:** the index bits must lie entirely inside the page offset. Otherwise
two virtual addresses for the same physical page could pick different sets — *synonyms*.

$$\text{sets} \times \text{line size} \le \text{page size}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
VIPT is the concrete instance of MIT's "part of the address is encoded in the location"
— and it is why that slogan has teeth. The index is computed from the virtual address
before anyone knows what physical page it is in.

Draw the two paths: the index path is short and goes straight to the SRAM; the tag path
goes through the TLB. They meet at the comparator. That is the whole trick, and it is
worth a proper diagram on the board.

The constraint in the box is the one that bites on the next slide.
:::

## The Open Question {.smaller}

Our 1 GHz caches: `256 sets × 64 B = 16 KB`. Our small page size: **4 KB**.

$$16\ \text{KB} > 4\ \text{KB}$$

So **two of the eight index bits come from the virtual page number**, not from the page
offset. Which means the hardware is either:

1. using "VIPT" loosely, and cacheable mappings must use **≥ 16 KB pages**;
2. doing something undocumented to handle synonyms; or
3. accepting aliasing, and relying on the OS never to create it.

::: {.fragment}
The manual does not say. **We do not know.** This is a real, checkable open question
about the chip in your hand — and a good one.
:::

::: {.notes}
Be scrupulous here: this is *our* derivation from two documented facts (the cache
geometry in §7.2 and the 4 KB page size in the MMU chapter), not a claim the manual
makes. The manual says VIPT; the arithmetic says the constraint is violated at 4 KB.

The most likely reading is (1) — cacheable regions use larger pages, and the MMU
supports 2 MB and 1 GB pages, which would make the constraint comfortably satisfied. But
"most likely" is not "documented", and saying so out loud is better teaching than
smoothing it over.

This is also a good exam question or a project: write a test that maps two virtual
addresses to the same physical page and measures whether the cache aliases.
:::

## Write-Back, Prefetch, and Adaptive Allocation {.smaller}

Three mechanisms on our D-cache that MIT's taxonomy does not contain:

- **Write-back** with a dirty bit — exactly as taught, no surprise.
- **Strided prefetch** — the LSU detects a miss pattern and prefetches up to 16 lines
  ahead, forward or backward. It manufactures spatial locality that is not there.
- **Adaptive write-allocate** — after *N* consecutive line writes (`HINT.AMRL1`), the
  page's write-allocate property switches **off** automatically.

::: {.fragment}
That last one is the `memset` problem, solved in hardware: if you are writing a whole
buffer, fetching each line before overwriting it is pure waste. The cache notices and
stops doing it.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide is the best answer to "why should I care about the textbook model if real
chips differ" — because the differences are all *refinements* of the model, and you
cannot see why they exist until you know what problem they solve.

Adaptive write-allocate is the clearest case. From the textbook you learn write-allocate
versus write-no-allocate is a static configuration choice. Real hardware makes it
dynamic, per page, based on observed behaviour, because neither static choice is right
for all code.

The prefetcher is worth a caveat: prefetching *manufactures* locality, which means the
locality principle is no longer purely an empirical fact about programs — hardware now
exploits access patterns that a naive working-set analysis would call random.
:::

# Part VI — Synthesis

## What We Actually Learned {.smaller}

1. **The hierarchy is forced.** A large fast memory cannot be built — latency grows with
   array size by physics. Stacking dies is the only recent escape.
2. **Locality is the load-bearing assumption.** If programs accessed memory uniformly,
   every technique here would be worthless.
3. **AMAT is the whole game.** `HitTime + MissRatio × MissPenalty`. Every mechanism in
   the lecture moves one of those three terms.
4. **Associativity, block size, and replacement are three answers to two questions.**
   How do we search, and whom do we evict.
5. **Our four cores are all on the same curves** — 2, 4, 8, 12 ways; 64-byte lines;
   none to 96 MB of L3.

::: {.fragment}
> The textbook model is not wrong. It is *under-specified* — and the places where real
> silicon fills in the gaps are exactly where the engineering lives.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read these as the examinable summary. Each one is a sentence a student should be able to
expand into a paragraph.

Claim 5 is the one that took the whole of Part V to establish, and it is the one worth
the most: they should leave able to look at any processor's spec sheet, read the cache
line, and say something intelligent about it.
:::

## Discussion Prompts {.smaller}

- The C906 I-cache is 2-way and its D-cache is 4-way. **Argue for or against** keeping
  them symmetric.
- The A53 has 32 KB + 32 KB + 128 KB; the C906 has 32 KB + 64 KB and no L2. **Which
  would you rather compile for**, and does the answer depend on the program?
- Adaptive write-allocate turns itself off under streaming stores. **What could go
  wrong** with a mechanism that changes policy based on observed history?
- The VIPT constraint appears to be violated at 4 KB pages. **Design an experiment**
  that would settle it.
- Given `AMAT = HT + MR × MP`, and a fixed transistor budget, **where do you spend it** —
  more ways, more sets, or an L2?

::: {.fragment}
Every one of these is answerable from the material in this deck. None has a single
right answer.
:::

::: {.notes}
These are designed to be argued in class or written as homework. The last one is the
best: it forces them to use the equation rather than recite it.

For the fourth, the experiment is: allocate two virtual pages, map them to the same
physical page, write through one and read through the other, and see whether the second
read sees the first write. If it does, no aliasing. That is a real test and it is
within reach of someone who can write a kernel module.

Do not answer them. Let the room do it.
:::
